title: Hayes's band forced out of Chicago by union rules
summary: Goodwin explains the Chicago local limited a visiting big band to a few weeks, which hurt them near the Grand Terrace.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, what happened back in the '30s, at that time I thought it was a bad thing when we went to Chicago on --
Whose band?
This was Thamon Hayes' and his band, and also later it became Harlan Leonard's band and the Kansas City Rockets. We were in Chicago and we wanted to --
Where were you playing?

We were playing for a guy named Sam Rifus at -- what was the name of the club? It was on Michigan Boulevard. It wasn't far from the Club DeLisa. Well anyway, we had what I thought was a great band and people thought so also.
You were playing for a white audience?
Well no, not so much. It was mixed, see because this was Chicago and Earl Hines would be down where we were playing every night.
Come down and listen to you play?
He was at the Grand Terrace.
I was just going to say those were the Grand Terrace days'.

Yeah, he was at the Grand Terrace and we were great enough so he didn't want us around and the union saw that we -- you know, we couldn't dicker with them no way but since that time -- I was young then, I can see being a union man myself, I can see why --
Well, you're a union official.
Yes, but to come into a place and you bring a band and --
Well, what was the problem? I mean, how could they --
Well, it's the same problem that it is now. You know, you just don't take an organized band in a territory that big and oust the rest of the musicians out of their jobs, you know.
Well, there are traveling bands. We had Les Brown last Sunday night at the --
A one nighter.
One nighter, yeah.
Yeah but we were on a steady job and the man --
You mean the union kicked you out of town?
Well, they had a -- their bylaws stated that you could come there and play I think it was two or three weeks.
Two weeks. And then what?
Then you had to go out and you could come back but we didn't have the money to .
Well how about the Four Tons were at the Frolcs in Chicago for a long time.
Well, this was a different thing.
Same local, same union.
Yeah but we were a big band and see
Yeah.

-- is quite a difference and they were playing more or less an act; it was more or less an act than a dance band. Well I can see their point, you know, you're going to have 12 musicians coming in here going to work, you know, when we've got 12 musicians could be playing in that same place.
Well now if you played two weeks and then took a week out --
You had to take longer than that.
You had to take longer than a week?
Yeah.
That's what I was going to ask, how long you had to take?
You had to take longer than that. I think it was a matter of months.
Anyway, you had to leave.

You leave and come back in see but the thing about it, if we'd had any backing, any money or anything, we could have stayed because see you can be there a certain length of time and you can join as a traveling --
Oh yeah.
-- musician. The same as now, you know.
